strengths: Broad and systematic empirical study: the paper evaluates 14 models across 3 model families (Llama-3, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5), spanning base and finetuned variants and multiple scales, which is more comprehensive than prior dormant-head analyses that examined only a few heads in one model.

The paper goes beyond classification to causal verification: zeroing out identified heads during MMLU evaluation with a random-ablation baseline provides a sound operational test of whether 'inactive' heads are actually removable.

The central finding is useful and well-supported: average head output norm (AHON, LN) is a more model-agnostic inactivity signal than first-token attention weight (AWFT), and AWFT underestimates inactive heads (~4.6% vs ~12.2% on average). This meaningfully corrects the picture painted by prior attention-weight-based work.

Analysis of score distributions (Wasserstein distances) yields additional insights, e.g., finetuning (SFT/DPO/RLHF) largely preserves attention head behavior, and scale effects emerge mainly at large model sizes.

Reproducibility is reasonably good: standard public models, lm-evaluation-harness, documented thresholds, PyTorch implementation listings, and extensive appendix figures (full per-model ablation curves, score distributions, IoU/precision matrices).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the proposed score functions: most are simple recombinations of previously studied quantities — value vector norms were already analyzed by Kobayashi et al. (2020) and Guo et al. (2024b) ('attention score is not all you need: value also matters'), and head output norm is a direct measure of what the paper itself states is the definition of inactivity. The 'taxonomy of 13 score functions' is largely 6 base metrics plus normalization variants, which inflates the apparent contribution.

Evaluation is narrow: all verification is done exclusively on MMLU (5-shot). The paper acknowledges head dormancy is context-dependent (Guo et al., 2024a), yet only one benchmark and one task type (MC log-likelihood) is used; generative, long-context, or perplexity-based evaluations are absent, leaving open whether the 1%-accuracy criterion holds more broadly.

The 1% MMLU accuracy tolerance is a weak bar for a benchmark where small perturbations are hard to detect, and no variance/seed analysis or statistical significance is reported; borderline results (e.g., improvements of +3 to +6 points on some models, small regressions on others) are hard to assess without uncertainty estimates.

Missing baselines from the pruning literature: no comparison against established head-importance/pruning methods (e.g., Michel et al. gradient-based importance, Voita et al. learned gates, Li et al. subset pruning), making it difficult to know whether thresholding AHON is actually competitive, only that it beats one attention-weight metric (AWFT).

Practical significance is limited and explicitly disclaimed: the intervention is dynamic per-forward-pass zeroing, which computes and stores attention weights/values anyway and yields no inference savings; the paper's own potential applications (efficiency, KV cache, compression) are not explored, so the contribution is purely analytical.

Some claims appear overclaimed relative to evidence, e.g., 'to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically evaluate the degree of head inactivity' ignores prior systematic dormant-head verification studies; conclusions about scale effects rest on the assumption that scale is the only variable, which the authors themselves admit is unverifiable.

strengths: The paper conducts a broad empirical study across 14 models from 3 model families, which is more extensive than prior head-dormancy work (Guo et al., 2024a) that examined only 3 heads in a single model.

The intervention-based validation (zeroing identified heads and measuring MMLU accuracy against a random ablation baseline) is a sound methodology for verifying that candidate 'inactive' heads are truly unnecessary, rather than relying purely on observational statistics.

The core observation — that attention-weight-based sink scores (AWFT) underestimate inactivity because head inactivity is better captured by output norms — is a useful corrective to recent attention-sink-driven narratives, and the IoU/precision analysis (Figure 2) supports that the proposed score functions identify distinct head subsets.
The paper includes reproducibility details: PyTorch implementations of the score functions, model/dataset specifics, and complete per-model results in the appendix.
The analysis of score distributions across finetuning stages (SFT/DPO/RLHF on OLMo-2) and model scales is an interesting secondary contribution.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the central finding that heads with small output norms contribute little is close to expected from the magnitude/importance-based pruning literature (Voita et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019; Kobayashi et al., 2020 already analyzed value-vector norms; Guo et al., 2024b explicitly argued 'value also matters'). The 'taxonomy' is a collection of simple threshold heuristics rather than a principled framework, and no learned or optimization-based importance criteria are compared against — only AWFT and random ablation.

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (MMLU, 5-shot). The 1%-of-baseline accuracy criterion is a fairly weak bar, and no error bars, seeds, or statistical significance are reported, despite MMLU accuracy fluctuations across eval settings often exceeding 1%.

The '12% of heads are inactive' headline claim is context-dependent: the paper's own Appendix A.4 (Figure 9) shows score distributions shift substantially between FineWeb-Edu and MMLU, yet the headline numbers are reported only on MMLU inputs. The dynamic per-forward-pass head selection also conflates dataset-specific behavior with a model-level property.

No efficiency or downstream-pruning demonstration is provided even though the abstract and introduction motivate the work via computational redundancy; the paper explicitly disclaims this ('our focus is strictly on understanding'), which limits practical significance.

Key confounds are acknowledged but not resolved: Qwen2.5 scale analysis assumes model scale is the only variable while admitting training-token counts are unknown; Llama-3.2 similarity to Llama-3.1 is explained by distillation, muddying the scaling conclusions.

The empirical contribution largely confirms an intuitive hypothesis (small-norm outputs can be zeroed with little loss) with simple heuristics; the incremental advance over Guo et al. (2024a) and Gu et al. (2025) — adding norm-based scores and scaling up the model count — may be insufficient for a top-tier venue.

Presentation issues: several typos ('their their score', 'proceeds' instead of 'precedes'), a truncated bibliography entry ('A Vaswani'), and Figure 2/3 heatmaps that are difficult to read, weaken clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and relevant question: how prevalent are truly inactive attention heads in pretrained LLMs, and how should 'inactivity' be measured? It convincingly argues that attention-weight-based characterizations (e.g., Avg Weight of First Token from Gu et al. 2024a/2025) are insufficient and that head output norms are a more model-agnostic signal.

The empirical scope is substantial: 14 models across 3 model families (Llama-3, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5), covering base, SFT, DPO, and RLHF variants, with intervention-based validation (zeroing heads during MMLU evaluation) rather than relying solely on observational score analysis.

The central quantitative findings are concrete and useful: on average >12% of heads can be zeroed within 1% of baseline MMLU accuracy vs. <5% identified by the prior attention-sink score, and Avg Head Output Norm (LN) ranks 1st for 8/14 models and top-3 for 13/14. These results directly correct prior claims about 'dormant' heads.

The analysis of score distributions (Wasserstein distances) yields additional interesting insights, e.g., that finetuning (SFT/DPO/RLHF) barely changes attention head behavior and that scale effects only appear at 14B, which is relevant to the interpretability community.

The paper is transparent and reproducible: it specifies thresholds, quantile-based selection, evaluation harness, model details, and includes PyTorch implementations in the appendix; the claim of dynamic (per-forward-pass) rather than static pruning is clearly delineated from prior pruning work.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the 13 score functions are simple hand-crafted statistics (norms, entropy) with thresholding; calling this a 'taxonomy' somewhat oversells what is essentially a set of heuristics. There is no learned, optimization-based, or gradient-based method.

Missing comparison against established head-importance/pruning baselines (e.g., Voita et al.'s stochastic gates, Michel et al.'s importance scores, gradient-based or L1 pruning methods). The paper compares mainly against AWFT, which is a weak baseline; it is unclear how a modern pruning importance criterion would perform under the same intervention protocol.

The evaluation criterion (MMLU accuracy within 1%) is narrow. Inactivity on a single multiple-choice benchmark does not establish that heads are inactive in general (e.g., for other capabilities, long-context tasks, or generation quality); the paper itself notes domain-dependence of dormancy (Guo et al., 2024a) but only validates on MMLU and FineWeb-Edu.

Despite framing around 'computational redundancy' and 'wasted head computation,' no efficiency results are reported (FLOPs, wall-clock latency, KV cache savings). The paper explicitly disclaims efficiency as a focus, but this weakens the practical significance of the findings and the impact of identifying 12% inactive heads.

No statistical rigor around results: no seeds/variance reporting for MMLU evaluations, no confidence intervals on the 1% accuracy threshold, and some claims (e.g., finetuning 'causes little to no change' in attention) rest on distribution-distance arguments that are not validated against a null/model-scale reference.

Some confounds are not fully addressed: head output norms vary systematically by layer/depth, and the LN normalization interacts with this; zeroing many heads in specific layers may act like depth pruning rather than head-level inactivity. The paper does not analyze where (which layers) the zeroed heads concentrate.

Scale and finetuning analyses rely on Qwen2.5/OLMo-2 checkpoints whose training data and token counts differ or are undisclosed, so the inference that 'model scale is the only variable' is speculative, as the authors partly acknowledge.

strengths: Thorough and systematic empirical study: 12 score functions evaluated across 14 models from 3 model families (Llama-3.x, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5), covering base, SFT, DPO, and instruction-tuned variants, giving unusually broad coverage for an analysis paper.

Claims are validated through interventions rather than score inspection alone: zeroing out identified heads and measuring MMLU/PIQA/WinoGrande accuracy provides a concrete, falsifiable test of inactivity, with a random-zeroing baseline for comparison.

The central finding is clear and useful: head output norm (AHON, LN) is more model-agnostic and dataset-stable than attention-weight-based scores (AWFT), which substantially underestimates inactivity (4.6% vs 12.2% on average). The layer-wise and sequence-length analyses (Figs. 5, 13-15) convincingly demonstrate AWFT's instability across datasets.

Additional analyses (Wasserstein distances of score distributions, finetuning invariance, scale effects, circuit-based head definition in A.1, PCA of attention matrices) add depth, and the appendix is unusually complete, including PyTorch implementations that support reproducibility.
The paper clearly articulates its scope (understanding, not efficiency) and honestly discusses limitations, including the fact that the best score function requires computing the head output itself.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the score functions are simple heuristics, and the general question of removable/redundant attention heads is well-trodden (Voita et al. 2019; Michel et al. 2019; Behnke & Heafield 2020). The main contribution is a comparative empirical characterization rather than a new method or theory.

The zeroing-out intervention with 'accuracy within 1%' on MMLU is a relatively coarse verification criterion. A head with near-zero output could still be functionally redundant but active (e.g., cancellations via W_O, as the authors themselves acknowledge in A.1); the paper does not probe more sensitive functional measures (e.g., log-loss deltas, generation quality, downstream multi-task evaluation) in the main body.

Main-body evaluation relies almost entirely on MMLU with a fixed 1% tolerance; PIQA/WinoGrande results are relegated to the appendix and include cases where the proposed scores actually underperform AWFT (e.g., -4.39 on Llama-3.2-3B/PIQA), which somewhat tempers the model-agnostic claim.

No demonstrated practical payoff: the best score function (AHON LN) requires computing the head output, so it cannot yield compute or memory savings by itself; the paper's value is confined to scientific understanding, and the efficiency/architecture implications remain speculative.

Some claims are slightly overstated relative to prior work (e.g., 'first to systematically evaluate the degree of head inactivity' versus the head-pruning literature), and the model-scale analysis (Section 4.5) rests on the assumption that Qwen2.5 models differ only in scale, which the authors admit is not verifiable from public information.
Context-dependence of inactivity (A.5) and generation-time behavior are acknowledged but unexplored, leaving open how well the conclusions extend beyond single forward passes on MC benchmarks.

strengths: Systematic and broad empirical coverage: 14 models across 3 model families (Llama-3, OLMo-2, Qwen2.5), including base, SFT, DPO, and Instruct variants, which strengthens the generality of the findings.

The core methodological move is sound: rather than trusting a single score function (the attention-sink-based AWFT metric from prior work), the authors verify identified heads through interventions (zeroing outputs and measuring MMLU accuracy), which is the right way to validate claims of 'inactivity'.

The paper clearly demonstrates that attention-weight-based signals (AWFT) underestimate head inactivity and are dataset/model sensitive (Figures 4-5), and that output-based scores are more stable and model-agnostic. This is a useful corrective to prior 'dormant head' characterizations.

Extensive appendices covering the circuit-based vs. pre-projection head output definition, multiple benchmarks (PIQA, WinoGrande), sequence-length analysis, score distributions, and PyTorch reference implementations support reproducibility and transparency.
The limitations are candidly acknowledged, including that the best score function (AHON (LN)) offers no actual inference-time compute savings.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and conceptual depth. The observation that many attention heads can be removed with little performance degradation is well-established since Voita et al. (2019) and Michel et al. (2019), which the authors themselves cite. The main contribution reduces to proposing six simple score functions (plus normalizations) and showing that head output norm correlates best with intervenability. The central finding—that heads with small outputs are the ones that can be zeroed—is close to tautological and does not yield mechanistic insight into why such heads arise or what (if anything) they do.

The 'inactive' definition is circular and conflates redundancy with inactivity. A head may be individually zeroable because it is redundant with another head (canceling or duplicating contributions), not because it is inactive. The paper does not disentangle these cases, yet its headline claim ('more than 12% of heads are inactive') rests entirely on the zeroing criterion. The discussion of W_O-induced cancellations in Appendix A.1 actually highlights this conflation rather than resolving it.

Missing comparison to established pruning/importance baselines. The intervention evaluation uses only the proposed score functions and a uniform random baseline. Standard head-importance methods (e.g., learned stochastic gates of Voita et al., iterative pruning, first-order importance scores from Michel et al.) are not evaluated, so it is unknown whether the proposed scores actually outperform existing cheap importance metrics, not just AWFT.

Practical significance is weak or absent. The paper explicitly disclaims any efficiency application, and concedes that the winning score function requires computing the head output itself, making the identified 'inactive' computation impossible to skip at inference. This leaves the contribution as interpretability/analysis only, but the analysis itself (score distributions, Wasserstein distances between models) is largely descriptive and presented as qualitative observations (e.g., 'Qwen2.5-14B looks different') without hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, or error bars.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. The '12% of heads are inactive' figure is a single-point accuracy tolerance (within 1% on MMLU) under one intervention scheme, varies widely across models (0.4%-20.6%), and changes substantially across benchmarks (21% on PIQA, 14% on WinoGrande), suggesting the 'prevalence' is not a stable property. Thresholds are quantile-calibrated to target a chosen fraction of heads, which partially embeds the outcome into the setup.

The finetuning and scaling analyses (Section 4.5) are thin. Concluding that 'finetuning causes little to no change in attention behavior' from Wasserstein distances of coarse per-head score distributions, and that 'scale does little until 14B' from a single confounded family (training token counts not publicly documented, as the authors admit), are under-supported for the emphasis given to them in the abstract.

Writing and presentation have avoidable flaws: a broken sentence in the abstract, inconsistent notation (N used both for sequence length and in Eq. 1 layer averages), figures with illegible axis labels (Figures 2, 6, 17), and loosely stated claims (e.g., 'to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically evaluate the degree of head inactivity') that ignore closely related pruning-by-output-magnitude literature such as Kobayashi et al. (2020), which they cite.

Given the paper explicitly positions itself away from efficiency and its analysis contributions are incremental over existing knowledge of head redundancy and attention sinks, the overall significance does not meet the bar of a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper systematically explores a well-motivated question: whether attention heads labeled 'inactive' by attention-weight-based metrics (attention sinks / dormant heads) actually are inactive. The core insight—that head inactivity should be measured through head outputs rather than attention weights—is supported by convincing intervention experiments across 14 models from 3 model families.

The evaluation methodology is sound: thresholding score functions and verifying identified heads via zero-out interventions on MMLU (with PIQA and WinoGrande as additional benchmarks), comparing against a random-ablation baseline, is a reasonable and interpretable way to validate 'inactivity' definitions.

Findings are concrete and actionable: on average 12% of heads can be zeroed while retaining accuracy within 1% of baseline, AHON (LN) is the most model-agnostic score function, and AWFT-based 'dormant' characterizations underestimate inactivity by ~7%. These results meaningfully update the picture painted by Guo et al. (2024a) and Gu et al. (2025).

The analysis of score-distribution stability across datasets (Figure 5), finetuning stages (SFT/DPO/RLHF), and model scales adds genuine interpretability value, showing AWFT is dataset-sensitive while AHON (LN) is stable.

The appendix is unusually thorough: a careful treatment of the circuit-based vs. pre-projection definition of head output (Table 3, Figure 7), complete results for all models/score functions, PyTorch implementations, sequence-length analyses, and an honest limitations section acknowledging that AHON requires computing the head output itself and that generation tasks were not analyzed.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest. The score functions are simple statistics (attention entropy, value-vector norms, head-output norms), and the conclusion that magnitude-based signals predict ablatability echoes long-standing observations from the pruning literature (Voita et al. 2019; Michel et al. 2019; Kobayashi et al. 2020). The paper does not compare against established pruning importance scores (e.g., Michel et al.'s importance estimates or loss-based head attribution), so it is unclear how much AHON (LN) actually improves over standard magnitude/heuristic pruning criteria rather than just over AWFT.

The headline '12% of heads are inactive' is somewhat circular: it is the maximum percentage of heads that can be zeroed while staying within 1% of baseline accuracy, searched over 12 score functions × 7 thresholds per function. Taking the max over many configurations on the same benchmark used for verification may overstate the robust, transferable fraction of inactive heads; no held-out threshold selection or error bars on MMLU accuracy are reported.

Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice log-likelihood benchmarks; effects on generation, long-context tasks, and downstream efficiency (the stated potential application) remain untested, limiting the significance and impact of the findings.

The scalability analysis in Section 4.5 relies on an unverified assumption that model scale is the only variable in the Qwen2.5 family (training token counts are undocumented), so conclusions about scale effects are speculative.

The practical utility of the best score function is limited by the authors' own admission: AHON requires computing the head output, so it cannot yield inference-time compute savings, which weakens the relevance to efficiency—a key motivation raised in the introduction.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'we are the first to systematically evaluate the degree of head inactivity' understates related work on head pruning and importance analysis, and the finetuning-invariance finding is broadly consistent with prior observations in the fine-tuning and pruning literature.
